title: Publications
text:
Preprints



Joint last author


Phantom genetic nurture: assortative mating accounts for most of the apparent association between parental genotypes and childhood cognitive performance


Malawsky, D.S., Hegemann, L., Wootton, O., Havdahl, A.K., Sunde, H.F., & Martin, H.C. (2026). bioRxiv.


Introduces RAVEL, a model that uses two independent polygenic scores, and shows that once assortative mating is modelled, parents’ genotypes explain less than 0.5% as much variance in children’s test scores as the child’s own genotype, down from 10% in naive trio analyses.


doi:10.64898/2026.09.01.748516




Family genetic risk scores for major psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diagnoses in the Norwegian population


Bjørndal, L.D., Valstad, M., Ayorech, Z., Eilertsen, E.M., van Jole, O., Sunde, H.F., Grande, T.J.M., Torvik, F.A., Kendler, K.S., & Ystrom, E. (2026). PsyArXiv.


Computes family-history-based genetic risk scores for ten diagnoses across 6.2 million Norwegian residents, finding that higher scores predict earlier onset and recurrence, that partners’ scores correlate, and that within-family genotype data largely support the method’s assumptions.


doi:10.31234/osf.io/4qtu5_v2




Why educational inequality runs in families: Genetics matter more than environment


van Bergen, E., Sunde, H.F., Rowland, C.F., Melby-Lervåg, M., & Torvik, F.A. (2025). PsyArXiv.


Using register data on 569,035 Norwegian children and extended family models, finds that the .31 correlation between parents’ education and children’s school achievement is 68% genetic, 12% parental environment and 20% environment shared with the extended family.


doi:10.31234/osf.io/rehdj_v1

title: Publications
text:
2026



First author


Are Spouses Similar in Divorce? Investigating Spousal Similarity in Couple-Shared Outcomes


Sunde, H.F., & Dierker, P. (2026). Twin Research and Human Genetics.


Shows how chaining in-laws lets an extended twin model separate spousal similarity from individual effects, finding in 353,210 Norwegian marriages that ignoring it inflates estimates of individual-level influences on divorce.


doi:10.1017/thg.2026.10050Bluesky thread




First author


Parental income and psychiatric disorders from age 10 to 40: a genetically informative population study


Sunde, H.F., Eilertsen, E.M., Kinge, J.M., Kleppestø, T.H., Nordmo, M., Caspi, A., Moffitt, T.E., & Torvik, F.A. (2026). Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry.


Across 2.5 million Norwegians, lower parental income is linked to nearly all psychiatric disorders, but the pattern is consistent with a causal effect only in adolescence, while shared family risk factors can fully explain it in adulthood.


doi:10.1111/jcpp.70022Bluesky threadBluesky thread (preprint)Open-access preprint




Investigating the analytical robustness of the social and behavioural sciences


Aczel, B., et al. (2026). Nature.


In a crowdsourced reanalysis of 100 published studies by independent analysts, only 34% of reanalyses reproduced the original result within a narrow tolerance, although 74% reached the same conclusion.


doi:10.1038/s41586-025-09844-9




Parenthood and mental health throughout the life course: A total population study


Andersen, M.L., Sunde, H.F., Hart, R.K., & Torvik, F.A. (2026). Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology.


Parents had a lower risk of mental disorders than childless adults from their thirties into old age, with larger gaps among men and people with less education, and the pattern held when comparing siblings and identical twins.


doi:10.1007/s00127-026-03091-7




The cost of caring: Gendered health and labor market effects of grandparenthood


Andersen, M.L., Hart, R.K., Sunde, H.F., Davies, N.M., & Torvik, F.A. (2026). Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.


Becoming a grandparent sharply raises respiratory infections in the first two years, and ten years on, employed grandmothers are 12% less likely to work full time, compared with 2% for grandfathers.


doi:10.1073/pnas.2535409123




Parental income in childhood and health outcomes across age groups: a register-based study from Norway


Reme, B.-A., Sunde, H.F., Torvik, F.A., Kinge, J.M., Strand, B.H., & Wörn, J. (2026). BMC Medicine.


People who grew up in low-income households see their GP more often at ages 10–59, most of all for psychological problems, and most of that gap disappears once their own education and income are taken into account.


doi:10.1186/s12916-026-04735-w




Prevalence of Bodily Distress Syndrome and Prediction of Patient Outcomes: Cohort Study of 3762 Individuals With Persistent Pain


Landmark, L., Sunde, H.F., Fors, E.A., Kennair, L.E.O., & Reme, S.E. (2026). European Journal of Pain.


Almost all patients at a tertiary pain clinic (92.5%) met the criteria for moderate or severe bodily distress syndrome, and those who did improved less in functioning over the following year.


doi:10.1002/ejp.70212




Multivariate maternal effects across the internalizing–externalizing spectrum in childhood: results from the Norwegian mother, father, and child cohort study


Eilertsen, E.M., Eftedal, N.H., Cheesman, R., Ayorech, Z., Ebeltoft, J.C., Sunde, H.F., Tandberg, A.D., Torvik, F.A., & Ystrom, E. (2026). Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry.


Mothers’ genes, acting through parenting, explain 7–18% of the variation in children’s behaviour problems, mostly through a single general factor, and leaving them out distorts estimates of children’s own genetic effects.


doi:10.1111/jcpp.70111




The attractive personality: Like me, but better


Kleppestø, T.H., Bendixen, M., Sunde, H.F., Zietsch, B., Harper, K.T., Karlsen, H., Stavang, M., Eftedal, N.H., & Kennair, L.E.O. (2026). Evolution and Human Behavior.


Among 538 Norwegian students, people wanted partners similar to themselves on the Big Five traits and especially on social dominance orientation, while low neuroticism was broadly preferred.


doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2025.106811

title: Publications
text:
2025



First author


Understanding indirect assortative mating and its intergenerational consequences for educational attainment


Sunde, H.F., Eilertsen, E.M., & Torvik, F.A. (2025). Nature Communications.


Family models using the partners of twins and siblings in 1.5 million Norwegians show that couples match on education mainly through indirect assortment, especially social homogamy, and that about 38% of parent–child similarity in education is environmental.


doi:10.1038/s41467-025-60483-0Bluesky threadTwitter/X thread




Cognitive Abilities and Educational Attainment as Antecedents of Mental Disorders: A Total Population Study of Males


Nordmo, M., Sunde, H.F., Kleppestø, T.H., Nordmo, M., Caspi, A., Moffitt, T.E., & Torvik, F.A. (2025). Psychological Science.


In 272,351 Norwegian conscripts, higher cognitive ability in late adolescence predicted a lower risk of almost every mental disorder studied at ages 36–40, even between brothers, and the link was strongest among men with little education.


doi:10.1177/09567976251347221




Beyond additive genetic effects: Explaining family resemblance in school performance across millions of pairs of Norwegian relatives


Eftedal, N.H., Eilertsen, E.M., Sunde, H.F., Kleppestø, T.H., Ystrom, E., & Czajkowski, N.O. (2025). Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.


Models with only additive genetic effects and assortative mating fit much of the data from 82 kinds of relatives, but systematically underestimate how alike identical twins, maternal relatives, in-laws and adoptive relatives are.


doi:10.1073/pnas.2419627122




Last author


Personality and fertility dynamics in Norway across four decades – Findings from the HUNT survey


Skirbekk, V., Blekesaune, M., & Sunde, H.F. (2025). Personality and Individual Differences.


Extraverted people had their first child earlier and had more children, while more neurotic people also started earlier but had fewer children, with stronger links in men.


doi:10.1016/j.paid.2024.112862

title: Publications
text:
2024



First author


Genetic similarity between relatives provides evidence on the presence and history of assortative mating


Sunde, H.F., Eftedal, N.H., Cheesman, R., Corfield, E.C., Kleppestø, T.H., Seierstad, A.C., Ystrom, E., Eilertsen, E.M., & Torvik, F.A. (2024). Nature Communications.


Polygenic scores of 47,135 Norwegian co-parents reveal assortative mating in nine of sixteen traits, and greater genetic variance among offspring for six of them, including educational attainment, indicates that family similarity is still increasing.


doi:10.1038/s41467-024-46939-9Twitter/X threadTwitter/X threadTwitter/X thread




Non-random mating patterns within and across education and mental and somatic health


Torvik, F.A., Sunde, H.F., Cheesman, R., Eftedal, N.H., Keller, M.C., Ystrom, E., & Eilertsen, E.M. (2024). Nature Communications.


Among all Norwegian first-time parents, partners are more alike in mental than in physical health, and adjusting for school grades or education reduces health similarity between partners by 30–40%.


doi:10.1038/s41467-024-54966-9




A nationwide analysis of 350 million patient encounters reveals a high volume of mental-health conditions in primary care


Caspi, A., Houts, R.M., Moffitt, T.E., Richmond-Rakerd, L.S., Hanna, M.R., Sunde, H.F., & Torvik, F.A. (2024). Nature Mental Health.


One in nine GP visits in Norway over 14 years involved a mental-health condition, a share exceeded only by musculoskeletal problems and on par with infections and heart and lung conditions.


doi:10.1038/s44220-024-00310-5




The diminishing association between adolescent mental disorders and educational performance from 2006–2019


Nordmo, M., Kleppestø, T.H., Reme, B.-A., Sunde, H.F., von Soest, T., & Torvik, F.A. (2024). JCPP Advances.


As ADHD and internalizing diagnoses among Norwegian adolescents more than doubled, the grade gap between diagnosed and undiagnosed students narrowed, pointing to changing diagnostic thresholds as one contributing factor.


doi:10.1002/jcv2.12239




Associations between pain intensity, psychosocial factors, and pain-related disability in 4285 patients with chronic pain


Landmark, L., Sunde, H.F., Fors, E.A., Kennair, L.E.O., Sayadian, A., Backelin, C., & Reme, S.E. (2024). Scientific Reports.


Insomnia and pain intensity were the strongest correlates of disability, and together with psychological distress and fatigue they accounted for about a quarter of its variation.


doi:10.1038/s41598-024-64059-8




Intergenerational transmission of ADHD behaviors: genetic and environmental pathways


Kleppestø, T.H., Eilertsen, E.M., van Bergen, E., Sunde, H.F., Zietsch, B., Nordmo, M., Eftedal, N.H., Havdahl, A., Ystrom, E., & Torvik, F.A. (2024). Psychological Medicine.


A children-of-twins-and-siblings design shows that parents and children resemble each other in ADHD behaviours mainly through shared genes, with parental behaviours themselves accounting for only about 2% of the variation.


doi:10.1017/S003329172300315X

title: Publications
text:
2023



The association between parental internalizing disorders and child school performance


Nordmo, M., Kleppestø, T.H., Sunde, H.F., Flatø, M., Demange, P., & Torvik, F.A. (2023). npj Science of Learning.


Nearly one in five Norwegian children has a parent diagnosed with anxiety or depression, and the gap in their school grades is much smaller between siblings and absent among adoptees, arguing against a strong causal effect.


doi:10.1038/s41539-023-00182-x

title: Publications
text:
2022



First author


The ADHD deficit in school performance across sex and parental education: A prospective sibling-comparison register study of 344,152 Norwegian adolescents


Sunde, H.F., Kleppestø, T.H., Gustavson, K., Nordmo, M., Reme, B.-A., & Torvik, F.A. (2022). JCPP Advances.


Adolescents with ADHD had grade point averages more than one standard deviation lower, still 0.6 lower when compared with their own siblings, and the relative deficit was larger for girls and for children of highly educated parents.


doi:10.1002/jcv2.12064




Sweet spot in music—Is predictability preferred among persons with psychotic-like experiences or autistic traits?


Lisøy, R.S., Pfuhl, G., Sunde, H.F., & Biegler, R. (2022). PLOS ONE.


A pre-registered study found that people differ in how predictable they like music to be, but found no support for a link between that preference and autistic or psychotic-like traits.


doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0275308

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
NB: This document is a work in progress.
Nobody sets out to write a sentence that others cannot read. Yet academic papers are full of them, and their writers rarely notice. A writer never reads their own sentences cold: they already know what each one means. The reader does not, and has to rebuild the thought from the words on the page.
Students pick up the habits honestly. They read papers written this way, mistake difficulty for the voice of scholarship, and copy it. The habits that make prose hard to read are specific, though, and so are the fixes. Here are seven.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Omit needless words
Due to the fact that is because. In order to is to. It is important to note that X is X. Delete the phrase and read the sentence again: if nothing is lost, nothing was there.
Apply the test upwards. A sentence that restates the one before it, a paragraph whose conclusion you drew two pages ago, a section that does not advance the argument: cut them rather than polish them.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Start where the reader is
Every sentence has two strong positions. The opening is read as what this is about, the close as the point. Old information belongs at the opening — usually whatever the last sentence ended on — and new information at the close, where it becomes the opening of the next.
Broken: Children’s education resembles their parents’ education. People tend to choose partners with a similar level of education. Advantage and disadvantage become concentrated in the same families.
Repaired: Children’s education resembles their parents’ education. Those parents also resemble each other, because people tend to choose partners with a similar level of education. That similarity between partners concentrates advantage and disadvantage in the same families.
The facts are the same. In the second version each sentence begins on the term the last one ended with, so the reader is never left holding a sentence in suspense, waiting to find out what it has to do with anything.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Name the actor
In the active voice the subject does the thing — the reviewer rejected the paper — and in the passive it has the thing done to it: the paper was rejected. The passive hides who did what. Mistakes were made names nobody. The sample was collected leaves the reader asking by whom. Write we collected the sample.
The passive has one defence: it lets a sentence open on old information when the actor is new. If the previous sentence ended on a questionnaire, the questionnaire was developed by a team of clinicians keeps the reader where they already are. That is the only reason to use it. Chosen for variety, or from a sense that impersonality sounds scientific, the passive voice costs clarity and readability.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Use verbs, not nouns
A nominalisation is a verb turned into a noun: analysis from analyse, measurement from measure, introduction from introduce.
A sentence is easiest to read when the subject is the actor and the verb is the action. Nominalisation moves the action into the subject, and leaves a weak verb behind — conduct, perform, carry out. Nominalisations are a key reason why academic writing is so hard to read.
So we performed an analysis of the data becomes we analysed the data. There was a reduction in the prevalence of depression following the introduction of the programme becomes depression became less common after we introduced the programme. Avoiding nominalisations also reduces the number of words, which is always a good thing.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Repeat yourself deliberately
Call the same thing a sample in one paragraph, a cohort in the next and a group in the third, and the reader must decide whether you mean one thing or three. Some will decide wrongly. Fix a term at first use and keep it. Repetition tells the reader that the referent has not changed.
Repeated structure does the same for comparisons. The first group received the drug; the second group received the placebo. Everything but the contrast is held constant, so attention falls on the one element that differs. Build the items of a list to a single grammatical pattern and the reader learns the shape once and spends the rest of their attention on the content. Break the pattern and the differences you did not intend compete with the one you did.
Repeat words and structure, not points. A point made twice is still a sentence to cut.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Formality is not obscurity
Being scientific means being honest, and honesty means writing so that a reader can check you. A claim that is hard to understand is hard to disagree with. First person, ordinary vocabulary, short sentences and the active voice are all compatible with serious scholarship. Use the long word when it is the exact one, and not otherwise.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
Writing is rewriting
A first draft is rarely a good draft. A first draft is for working out what you think; the habits above apply to the second, the third and the fourth, and a plain sentence is usually the fourth version of itself.
The rest is practice, and practice means reading with attention. When a paragraph of someone else’s is easy to follow, stop and work out what makes it so; when you lose the thread, work out why. The diagnosis is what you keep — noticing that a paragraph works teaches you nothing until you can say why it works. Then do the same to your own drafts, which is harder, because you already know what you meant.

title: Academic writing doesn’t have to be hard to read
text:
A full example
Broken: Due to the fact that the quality of student writing is of considerable importance, an investigation of the effects of feedback was undertaken by our research group. A total of 120 participants were recruited. Random allocation of the respondents to two conditions was then performed. Detailed comments were given to the first cohort, whereas only a grade was received by the other set of students. An improvement in the revision quality of the first group was observed, in contrast to the second group, where no such improvement was found. It should be noted that the finding that feedback improves revision is an important one.
Repaired: Feedback is meant to improve how students revise, but it is not clear what kind of feedback does. We recruited 120 students and assigned them at random to two groups. The first group received detailed comments; the second group received only a grade. When the students revised their work, only the first group improved.
The repair names the researchers (“we”), puts the action back in the verbs, calls the students one thing throughout, gives the two groups the same sentence shape, and ends on the result instead of on a claim that the result matters. None of these changes set out to make it shorter, yet the repair runs to 54 words against the original’s 104.

title: Hans Fredrik Sunde
text:
I am a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Fertility and Health, Norwegian Institute of Public Health, where I work on a project called PARMENT – Parenthood, childlessness, and mental health in times of falling fertility.
I primarily investigate causes and consequences of partner similarity (such as assortative mating), and its consequences for social differences, mental health, and genetic methodology. I also investigate associations between social differences and mental health across generations, attempting to differentiate selection and causation. My interests include behavioral genetics, psychology, statistics, philosophy of science, and methodological issues in social science.
I have a PhD in psychology, which I attained when I defended my dissertation Reproduction of socioeconomic differences and mental health across generations the spring of 2024 at the University of Oslo’s (UiO) Department of Psychology. Previously, I have a master’s degree in psychology from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), which specialized on learning; brain, behavior and environment.
Follow me on LinkedIn, BlueSky (@hfsunde.bsky.social), and the other place (@hfsunde).

title: Hans Fredrik Sunde
text:
Selected papers





Understanding indirect assortative mating and its intergenerational consequences for educational attainment


Sunde, H.F., Eilertsen, E.M., & Torvik, F.A. (2025). Nature Communications.


Abstract



We develop a framework for understanding indirect assortative mating and provide updated definitions of key terms. We then develop family models that use partners of twins and siblings to freely estimate the degree of genetic and social homogamy, and account for it when investigating sources of parent-offspring similarity. We applied the models to educational attainment using 1,545,444 individuals in 212,070 extended families in the Norwegian population and Norwegian Twin Registry. Partner similarity in education was better explained by indirect assortment than direct assortment on observed educational attainment, with social homogamy being particularly important. The implied genotypic partner correlation (r = 0.34) was comparable to earlier studies, and higher than expected under direct assortment. About 38% of the parent-offspring correlation (r = 0.34) was attributable to various forms of environmental transmission. Alternative models that assumed direct assortment estimated environmental transmission to be lower, but these did not fit the data well.



doi:10.1038/s41467-025-60483-0Bluesky threadTwitter/X thread







Genetic similarity between relatives provides evidence on the presence and history of assortative mating


Sunde, H.F., Eftedal, N.H., Cheesman, R., Corfield, E.C., Kleppestø, T.H., Seierstad, A.C., Ystrom, E., Eilertsen, E.M., & Torvik, F.A. (2024). Nature Communications.


Abstract



Assortative mating – the non-random mating of individuals with similar traits – is known to increase trait-specific genetic variance and genetic similarity between relatives. However, empirical evidence is limited for many traits, and the implications hinge on whether assortative mating has started recently or many generations ago. Here we show theoretically and empirically that genetic similarity between relatives can provide evidence on the presence and history of assortative mating. First, we employed path analysis to understand how assortative mating affects genetic similarity between family members across generations, finding that similarity between distant relatives is more affected than close relatives. Next, we correlated polygenic indices of 47,135 co-parents from the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and found genetic evidence of assortative mating in nine out of sixteen examined traits. The same traits showed elevated similarity between relatives, especially distant relatives. Six of the nine traits, including educational attainment, showed greater genetic variance among offspring, which is inconsistent with stable assortative mating over many generations. These results suggest an ongoing increase in familial similarity for these traits. The implications of this research extend to genetic methodology and the understanding of social and economic disparities.

Are Spouses Similar in Divorce? Investigating Spousal Similarity in Couple-Shared Outcomes


Sunde, H.F., & Dierker, P. (2026). Twin Research and Human Genetics.


Abstract



In behavioral genetics, divorce is typically analyzed as an individual-level outcome, even though marital dissolution can only be experienced by couples. In this article, we discuss how assortative mating complicates the study of couple-shared outcomes because individual-level effects can be confounded by effects of the spouse. We then show how chain-linking affines (i.e., in-laws) provides sufficient information to estimate spousal similarity for couple-shared outcomes, which we incorporate into an extended twin model that we use to test for sex differences and assortative mating for individuals’ liability to divorce. We linked the Norwegian twin register to the Norwegian population register and constructed 124,544 extended family units (1196 units with monozygotic twins) comprising 353,210 marriages entered between 1983 and 2008. We found that divorce was significantly correlated among affines, and that female relatives were more highly correlated than male relatives. The extended twin model estimated a strong correlation (r = .60, SE = .10) between female and male familial factors. Couples’ liability to divorce was attributed to 18% (SE = 5%) female and 10% (SE = 3%) male familial factors, with an additional 16% (SE = 4%) accounted for by their correlation. Estimates from a classic twin model were considerably higher. These findings show that spousal similarity is an important source of variation in divorce liability and that failing to model it can inflate estimates of individual-level effects. Overall, the analytical framework offers a blueprint for dissecting any couple-shared outcome into sex-specific and assortative components.

Parental income and psychiatric disorders from age 10 to 40: a genetically informative population study


Sunde, H.F., Eilertsen, E.M., Kinge, J.M., Kleppestø, T.H., Nordmo, M., Caspi, A., Moffitt, T.E., & Torvik, F.A. (2026). Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry.


Abstract



Background. Lower parental income is associated with more psychiatric disorders among offspring, but it is unclear if this association reflects effects of parental income (social causation) or shared risk factors (social selection). Prior research finds contradictory results, which may be due to age differences between the studied offspring.


Methods. Here, we studied psychiatric disorders in the entire Norwegian population aged 10 to 40 years between 2006 and 2018 (N = 2,468,503). By linking tax registries to administrative health registries, we described prevalence rates by age, sex, and parental income rank. Next, we grouped observations into age groups (adolescence, ages 10–20 years; early adulthood, 21–30 years; adulthood, 30–40 years) and applied kinship‐based models with extended families of twins and siblings to decompose the parent–offspring correlation into phenotypic transmission, passive genetic transmission, and passive environmental transmission.


Results. We found that lower parental income rank was associated with higher prevalence of nearly all psychiatric disorders, except for eating disorders, for both men and women at all ages from 10 to 40 years. Comparing the top with the bottom paternal income quartile, the prevalence ratio of any psychiatric disorder was 0.47 among 10‐year‐olds and decreased to 0.72 among 40‐year‐olds. The parent–offspring correlation was −.15 in adolescence, −.10 in early adulthood, and −.06 in adulthood. The kinship‐based models indicated that phenotypic transmission could account for 39% of the parent–offspring correlation among adolescents (p < .001), but with no significant contribution in early adulthood (p = .181) or adulthood (p = .737). Passive genetic and environmental transmission contributed to the parent–offspring correlation in all age groups (all p’s < .001).


Conclusions. Our findings are consistent with a significant role of social causation during adolescence, while social selection could fully explain the parent–offspring correlation in adulthood.
